summary: Gives definitions and considerations for operating an X.500 Directory Service in the United States. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A big public phone and address book run by many groups together. This explains what you should think about when running one in one country.

subtitle: Practical, legal and organizational advice for setting up an X.500 white pages directory in the US.

tldr.problem: Organizations in the US wanted to run an electronic white pages directory and join a wide-area one, but faced technical, legal and data management choices with little guidance.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains the X.500 directory and information models, summarizes legal issues such as user rights, data integrity and security, describes the Internet White Pages pilot infrastructure, and ends with recommendations.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational snapshot from May 1996 based on experience in the Internet White Pages project. It sets no standard and says security issues are not discussed in its own security section.

today: RFC 1943 is an Informational memo from May 1996, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its figures and descriptions of providers reflect the time it was written.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
RFC 1943 is an introduction for people planning a directory service for an organization in the US. It covers technical, legal and organizational aspects and illustrates the options with examples of current X.500 service providers. It comes from work for the Integrated Directory Services Working Group in the IETF.

A directory serves a list of information, defined by its purpose, about people, organizations, services or network hardware. The aim of X.500 is to make using the directory as easy as calling directory assistance. It is an international standard ratified by ISO and the ITU-T (formerly CCITT) in 1988. The memo argues that a global electronic white pages helps email, since users can find addresses by common name, surname and organization.
sections.plainLanguage: An electronic phone book is easier to keep up to date than a paper one, and lots of groups can share one big book if they follow the same rules.

sections.title: The X.500 Directory Model
sections.content:
X.500 is a distributed collection of independent systems that together provide one logical database. Information about an organization is kept locally in a Directory System Agent (DSA), and DSAs exchange information using the X.500 protocol. A Directory User Agent (DUA) is what a person or program uses to reach DSAs; it may be an IP protocol such as whois or finger, or a graphical application.

Connected DSAs form the Directory Information Tree (DIT). In the QUIPU-based pilot a root represents the world, with countries below it, then organizations, then organizational units and people. An organization is free to run a stand-alone system, or to keep information for other organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each organization keeps its own page of the phone book on its own computer, and the computers can ask each other for missing pages. A DUA is the window you look through to ask.

sections.title: Entries, Attributes and Names
sections.content:
All information is stored in entries, each belonging to at least one object class. For white pages these are country, organization, organizational unit and person. The object class decides which attributes an entry has, some mandatory and some optional. A Directory schema sets the rules for attributes. For the Person class, the mandatory attributes are objectClass, commonName and surName.

Each entry has a relative distinguished name (RDN) that uniquely identifies it. The RFC's example is @c=US@o=Sandia National Laboratory@ou=Employees@cn=Barbara Jennings. An organization chooses a DIT that suits it, typically one that resembles the organization itself. A complex tree can slow searches, especially with flat files rather than a database. The memo points to RFC 1274 for recommended schema.
sections.plainLanguage: Every card in the book has a type, such as person or company, and the type decides what lines the card has. A card's name is the path of boxes it sits inside.

sections.title: Legal Issues and User Rights
sections.content:
At the time, the US had no specific legal rules for information in an electronic directory. Personal information was freely transferred and largely unregulated unless the provider was an agency or held sensitive data, and rules differ for each state. Other countries may have stricter laws, so the memo says administrators should review them before importing data.

It recommends stating the directory's purpose clearly, since all data presented must fit it. It points to the North American Directory Forum User Bill of Rights, including the right to be told of inclusion and to examine and correct one's entry. It also covers data integrity, citing RFC 1355, and data security tools such as access control lists and limits on entries returned, noting these also affect legitimate users.

The minimum conditions it lists are: define the purpose, inform registrants, prevent use beyond the purpose, limit attributes to the purpose, work toward suitable security, and develop a way to correct or remove faulty data.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you put people in a phone book, you should tell them, only list what the book is for, let them fix mistakes, and keep strangers from copying the whole thing.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Pilot Projects
sections.content:
The White Pages Project, operated by Performance Systems International (PSI), provides a QUIPU infrastructure for sites that want their own X.500 directory. It began in 1989 as the NYSERNet White Pages Pilot Project, the first production-quality field test of OSI technology on top of TCP/IP. The memo reports participation from more than 30 countries with over 1 million entries.

The primary DSA, named Alpaca, is master for the DSAs of 117 organizations under c=US, with redundancy from Fruit Bat (PSI) and Pied Tamarin (InterNIC) and nightly slave updates. Other providers described are the InterNIC, which held data for 52 organizations as of June 1995, and ESnet, with over 120,000 entries.

On the client side, DUAs once needed the entire OSI stack. The memo describes LDAP, which runs directly over TCP and is used by nearly all X.500 clients, as the lighter route.
sections.plainLanguage: A few groups ran the first shared phone books and let others join. Early on you needed heavy software to read them, until a lighter way to ask came along.

sections.title: Recommendations for Getting Started
sections.content:
The memo advises a systematic approach and a cooperative effort among technical, administrative, organizational and legal staff. Smaller organizations can use a provider to run their DSA remotely, while those with expertise can run their own or join a white pages project.

The questions to settle first are: who are the customers, and will they cross country boundaries; what the contents should be, which must relate directly to the purpose; and what rights individuals have, at least inclusion by choice, access, and correction of inaccurate entries. Data should be maintained as corporate information, with regular accuracy checks and, for time-sensitive data, an attribute showing the last maintenance date.

It concludes that executive commitment is essential, that operational procedures must be clearly defined, and that people will only use the service if the information is consistent and accurate.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you start, decide who the book is for, what goes in it and what rights people in it get. Then check regularly that the information is still right.

items.title: DSA
items.text: Directory System Agent: holds the directory data for an organization.

items.title: DUA
items.text: Directory User Agent: lets a person or program query DSAs.

items.text: Directory Information Tree: the hierarchy formed by connected DSAs.
